title: How a Transistor Controls Current Explained Simply | PUC Electronics
description:
At the college fest Aarav taps a tiny microphone and the huge speakers boom across the ground. How can such a tiny signal control such a big current? With a bipolar junction transistor: like a small tap on a big water pipe, a small current controls a big one.

We build the transistor layer by layer: emitter (heavily doped, sends the carriers), base (very thin and lightly doped) and collector (the largest layer, it gets rid of heat), with the emitter base and collector base junctions. Then npn and pnp, and the symbol arrow on the emitter (npn: not pointing in). Inside an npn transistor the emitter base junction is forward biased and the collector base junction reverse biased: electrons cross the thin base like runners on an almost empty field, a few recombine (the small base current) and most reach the collector. On a live breadboard the scope shows a small change in base current making a big change in collector current, and we derive IE = IB + IC. Worked example, the exam trap, where it is asked, an original board pattern practice question with a full solution, and a formula card to screenshot.
